title: Remove Sub-Folders from the Filesystem
description:
You are given an array `folder` of distinct absolute folder paths. Each path starts with `/` and is made of one or more segments of lowercase letters separated by `/`, such as `"/a/bc/d"`.

A folder is a **sub-folder** of another listed folder `p` if its path starts with `p` followed by a `/`. Note that `"/a/bc"` is **not** a sub-folder of `"/a/b"`: the match must end on a segment boundary.

Remove every folder that is a sub-folder of some other folder in the list and return the remaining folders **sorted in ascending lexicographic order**.

**Example 1:**
```
Input: folder = ["/lib","/lib/js","/src/app","/src/app/ui","/src/db"]
Output: ["/lib","/src/app","/src/db"]
Explanation: "/lib/js" lives inside "/lib" and "/src/app/ui" lives inside "/src/app", so both are removed.
```

**Example 2:**
```
Input: folder = ["/var","/var/log/nginx","/var/log/app/old"]
Output: ["/var"]
Explanation: Both deeper folders sit somewhere under "/var", even though "/var/log" itself is not listed.
```

**Example 3:**
```
Input: folder = ["/usr/bin","/usr/binx","/usr/lib"]
Output: ["/usr/bin","/usr/binx","/usr/lib"]
Explanation: "/usr/binx" starts with the characters "/usr/bin" but not at a segment boundary, so nothing is removed.
```

examples.explanation: "/lib/js" lives inside "/lib" and "/src/app/ui" lives inside "/src/app", so both are removed.
Both deeper folders sit somewhere under "/var", even though "/var/log" itself is not listed.
"/usr/binx" starts with the characters "/usr/bin" but not at a segment boundary, so nothing is removed.

constraints: folder[i] contains only lowercase English letters and '/', starts with '/', and has no empty segments or trailing '/'
All entries of folder are unique
solution_approach: Brute force: for each folder, test it against every other folder to see whether some other path plus '/' is its prefix, giving O(n^2 * L) time. Better: build a trie keyed by path segments, marking the node where each folder ends. For each folder walk its segments; if you pass through a marked node before the last segment, it is a sub-folder and is dropped. Collect the survivors and sort them. Equivalently, sorting the paths first places every sub-folder right after its ancestor, so a single pass keeping the last kept root and checking startsWith(root + '/') also works. Both run in O(n * L * log n) time dominated by the sort (the trie walk itself is O(n * L)), with O(n * L) space.
hints: A folder path is a sequence of segments, not just a string of characters. Think about what it means to share a prefix segment by segment.
Insert each path into a trie where each edge is one segment, and mark the node where a folder ends. A folder is redundant if its walk crosses a marked node before reaching its own end.
Alternatively, sort the paths: every sub-folder then appears after its ancestor. Keep the last kept folder and drop the current one if it starts with that folder followed by '/'.
follow_up_questions: How would you also report, for each remaining folder, how many sub-folders were removed under it?
How would you handle paths that may contain '.' and '..' segments that must be normalised first?
